title: Isack Hadjar: “We looked stupid” in Las Vegas as I don’t like slipstreaming
article_text:
Isack Hadjar has admitted to underperforming in qualifying for Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix due to not realizing how powerful the tow would be on this high-speed street circuit.

Hadjar was 0.67s slower than Red Bull team-mate Max Verstappen in Q2 and 0.44s adrift in Q3 as he ended up down in fifth, and the gap may be partly down to his personal preferences as he told Sky Sports F1 he “just didn’t really focus on having a tow”.

“We had no tow,” the sophomore then told written media. “We looked a bit stupid out there for the final run, but the other teams played it very smart, parking the car in Turn 1 while we were exiting the pits. In the end, I saw I was alone. [My final] lap was good, but you're just useless down the straight, so I preferred to just abort.”

Asked by Motorsport.com if it was about playing the games a bit better next time, Hadjar replied: “I don't really like those games anyway. I like driving the car faster. It's just things you can't really control, it's a bit like rolling the dice.

“I don't really care. As long as I know I was quicker around the corners, I'm happy about that.”

Yet, Verstappen’s experience made it clear how crucial slipstreaming could be.

“The tow around here is crazy, because I was actually close to getting knocked out in Q2,” the Dutchman said. “Then I went out on my final lap and I was four or four-and-a-half seconds behind the car, and I gained like seven or eight tenths on the lap while not actually gaining that much in the corners. That just tells you how much you actually gain around the lap if you have a decent tow.”

Despite failing to improve on his second Q3 attempt, meaning he dropped from fourth to fifth, Hadjar will start fourth with Verstappen inheriting pole position, courtesy of pacesetter Kimi Antonelli’s five-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allowance.

“In the end, we're starting fourth tomorrow, so we're in a good position for a podium,” the Frenchman optimistically commented. “I think it's a track where you can easily overtake with these massive straights, with the current regulations. So P4, P5, P2… It doesn't really matter in the end, so I'm happy.”

title: Lewis Hamilton: With #1 driver backing at key points, we could have beaten Kimi Antonelli this season
article_text:
For Ferrari fans. The latest Scuderia Ferrari F1 news, driver updates, technical analysis and race reaction from Maranello and beyond.

Seven-time Formula 1 champion Lewis Hamilton believes he could have beaten Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli in their battle earlier in the season had he been given more support from Ferrari.

The Briton was speaking after the Las Vegas Grand Prix, where he had another clash with his team-mate Charles Leclerc, which sent him into a spin. He recovered to finish seventh, while Leclerc was penalised and finished 10th.

Asked about 1996 F1 champion Damon Hill's suggestion that Ferrari should make him its number one driver, Hamilton said he had never asked for that status, but felt he had needed it earlier in the year.

"I've never asked to be number one. I genuinely haven't ever asked," Hamilton said.

He pointed to a stage of the season when he was well clear of Leclerc and the nearest driver to challenge Antonelli for the title.

"I was second for a long time in the year, and at that point I needed backing to make sure we beat Kimi. There were a few circumstances in the season where, with the support, we could have beaten Kimi," he said.

After the 41-year-old claimed his first grand prix win with Ferrari in Barcelona in June, he was second in the drivers' standings, 41 points behind Antonelli and 40 points ahead of Leclerc. He was also second after Monaco, Belgium and Hungary.

Photo by: Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images

Antonelli went on to secure the championship at the Mexican Grand Prix, one week before Mercedes won the constructors' title, and now has 402 points to Hamilton's 267.

"I don't know, but it's not something I want to get into," he said when asked where his relationship with his team-mate goes from here. "These are questions that people are asking. At the end of the day, I performed as hard as I could, and I've been giving everything I could to get those points today.

"We were just constantly hit with challenges, and I just kept my head down."

Earlier in the race, Hamilton had been handed a 10-second penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage over McLaren's Lando Norris.

"10 seconds was insane and very, very harsh," he continued. "I was avoiding colliding with them, and they could have just told me to give the place back. A 10-second [penalty] is nuts. But I came back and I got back into the fight, and I could see Max up ahead and I was like, we're back in the fight.

"I was fighting with McLaren, so I honestly thought that I could maybe fight for a podium, and I'm literally only thinking about fighting McLaren, because that's where we need to be to get the second."

‘It’s nice to be back here’ - Megan Bruce celebrates return to the podium in Las Vegas Reverse Grid Race
article_text:
Megan Bruce was delighted to return to the F1 ACADEMY podium in Las Vegas, admitting that the difficult track conditions had caught her by surprise before she recovered to finish third in the Reverse Grid Race.

The TAG Heuer driver claimed her first podium since Montreal after overcoming a challenging start, with the cold temperatures and limited grip around the Las Vegas Strip Circuit making the opening laps particularly difficult and dropping her down to P7.

“Firstly it’s nice to be back here (in the podium positions),” she said. “I feel like it’s been a long time and that’s not really representative of the season we’ve had.

“It was very tricky at the start, obviously it’s really cold down here in Vegas and it’s a street track so the tarmac is really difficult. I definitely thought there’d be a lot more grip than this, which caught me by surprise in the first few laps. Then, we found a bit more of a rhythm throughout the race and got in a nice battle and made some moves up.”

With both Free Practice and Qualifying taking place in damp conditions, Bruce explained that the change in track conditions had made it difficult to judge the available grip, identifying her approach to the opening corner as the biggest lesson to take into the Feature Race on Saturday.

“Definitely to not over-push on the first lap, on the first corner,” she explained. “We had Free Practice and Qualifying which was quite damp, and in Quali there was a dry line but it was not the lap times we had now, so the conditions were very different.

“It’s good to know this now for the Reverse Grid Race because we're starting P3 (in the Feature Race), so it’s good to have these lessons now and prepare for tomorrow.”

Bruce's podium also keeps her in contention for Top Rookie honours, although the Campos Racing driver faces a considerable challenge heading into the final race. Payton Westcott leads the rookies on 78 points, with Natalia Granada on 59 and Bruce just one point further back on 58.

While acknowledging that some results have not reflected her pace throughout the season, Bruce remains determined to make the most of her final opportunity, with Campos also fighting to secure the Teams' title.

“We’ve still had a strong season, some things haven’t gone our way so it will be a bit more difficult but I think overall we’ve had a good season.

“If we could finish top rookie, that would be representative of our pace throughout. And obviously we’re still fighting for the Teams’ title so that’s another thing to take care of.”

title: What the teams said – Race day in Las Vegas
article_text:
Verstappen drove a masterclass in Las Vegas to record his third win here and fourth of the season. He led off the line, but was soon challenged by those behind having a tow. Despite losing the lead multiple times, every time the Dutchman kept calm and retook the place. Russell, Norris and Antonelli threw everything they could at the Red Bull man, but no one could make it stick.

Verstappen even had enough composure to debate deployment strategies with the team, worried about being passed last on the final lap and not having time to come back at his rival. But Antonelli’s late issue meant the last lap was the only one where Verstappen had some breathing room from the entire race.

As for Hadjar, his pace was very strong. He ran second and even challenged Verstappen at times. He looked on for a podium until he suffered an apparent front wing failure late on, the resultant pit stop dropping him out of the points. The Frenchman was also handed a 10-second post-race penalty for slowing down before the pit stops, as he attempted to create a gap with Red Bull double stacking their drivers.

“It was definitely one of the craziest Grands Prix I’ve ever experienced. The whole race was about managing the deployment, timing everything correctly and making sure you stayed ahead of the cars behind. They were constantly changing their strategy as well, so you always had to be aware of what was happening around you and make the right decisions. I just wanted to stay in the lead and not drop back into the pack. It was very unusual today and something completely different to what we normally experience, but the most important thing is that we won. We’ve been strong over the last few races, consistently scoring podiums, and the turnaround from the team has been very positive. We did everything right today and I’m happy we came away with the win.”

“A disappointing end to what was a really promising first half of the race. The start was great, and it was fun to be part of what was a crazy battle. We were fighting at the front and had a lot of pace. Unfortunately, the front wing took unexpected damage and we had to box, which took us out of the fight for at least a podium. We knew we’d be fast here, and we were. The car felt so strong through the corners and, with the natural tow, we were able to keep up on the straights. It’s a shame, as everything was looking great, but that’s racing sometimes.”

“What an incredible race and an outstanding performance from Max and the entire Team. We knew that energy management and the slipstream would play a significant role today, but I don't think anyone anticipated quite so much overtaking. Max was simply exceptional, both in attack and defence, keeping his composure right until the very last lap. The communication between Max, his engineers and the pit wall was outstanding, and that teamwork made a real difference in such an unpredictable race.

"At the same time, it is a real shame for Isack. He had fantastic pace, was right up there with Max and at one stage we were running P1 and P2. He deserved so much more from this weekend, and we owe him an apology for what happened today. we will analyse what happened with his front wing and come back stronger in Doha.

"We started the weekend on the back foot, but the way everyone responded, took risks and worked together to turn things around was remarkable. This victory is another fantastic reward for the hard work of everyone in the Team.

"We will enjoy the moment tonight, but then our focus will turn to the last two races of the season and trying to perform at that level again there.”

Norris started from P3, but he struggled on the soft tyres and dropped all the way out of the top 10 in the first stint. Piastri was going better on the mediums and soon climbed back into the top 10 and was even running ahead of his team mate at times. Somehow despite multiple moves, those two kept their battles clean.

The Australian lost out in the double stack behind the Safety Car, but soon climbed back to where his team mate was running. On the mediums, they looked much more competitive and weaved their way forward, with Norris even picking off Russell and Verstappen and leading for a few corners at one point.

They were behind the two Mercedes cars when Russell ran off, and both picked off Antonelli right at the end to score what, at times this weekend, looked a very unlikely double podium.

“It was a chaotic race from start to finish, and every lap brought something to manage: battery use, positioning, slipstreams and whether to attack or defend. I was down the order early on, and it took time to understand how to use the battery and get the most from the car. Once we worked that out, we started making progress. The cornering speed was strong, but our lack of straight-line speed made it difficult to move forward and hold position. We timed the opportunities well, especially in the closing laps, and second place was the best we could achieve. I’m very happy for the team to come away with a double podium.
